0: May he protect us both. May he nourish us both. May we work together with strength. May what we study shine. May we never resent each other. Om, peace, peace, peace.
1.1.1: Wanting the fruit of a great rite, Vajashravasa gave away everything he owned. He had a son named Nachiketa.
1.1.2: He was still a boy, but as the gifts were led away, faith came into him, and he thought:
1.1.3: These cows have drunk their last water, eaten their last grass, given their last milk, and will bear no more calves. Joyless are the worlds a man goes to who gives gifts like these.
1.1.4: He said to his father, "Father, to whom will you give me?" He asked a second time, and a third. His father said, "I give you to Death."
1.1.5: Of many, I go first. Of many, I go in the middle. What work does Yama have that he will do through me today?
1.1.6: Look at how those before us went, and see how those after us will go. A mortal ripens like grain, and like grain is born again.
1.1.7: A Brahmin guest comes into a house like fire. People calm that fire with an offering. Bring water, son of Vivasvat.
1.1.8: Hope and expectation, friendship and kind words, rites and good works, sons and cattle: the man of little sense loses them all when a Brahmin stays in his house without food.
1.1.9: Brahmin, you are a guest who deserves respect, and you have stayed three nights in my house without food. I bow to you; may it go well with me. In return, choose three wishes.
1.1.10: Death, let Gautama, my father, be calm in his mind and kind to me, his anger gone. When you send me back, let him know me and speak to me. Of the three, this is my first wish.
1.1.11: Auddalaki Aruni, your father, will know you as before. Sent back by me, seeing you freed from the mouth of death, he will sleep well at night, his anger gone.
1.1.12: In the world of heaven there is no fear at all. You are not there, and no one fears old age. Past hunger and thirst, beyond sorrow, one is glad in heaven.
1.1.13: Death, you know the fire that leads to heaven. Teach it to me, since I have faith. Those who reach heaven share in the deathless. This I choose as my second wish.
1.1.14: I will tell you; listen and understand, Nachiketa. I know the fire that leads to heaven. Know that fire, the way to endless worlds and their support, as hidden in the cave of the heart.
1.1.15: He told him of the fire that begins the worlds: which bricks, how many, and how to lay them. Nachiketa said it all back as it was told. Pleased with him, Death spoke again.
1.1.16: Delighted, the great one said: Here I give you one more wish today. This fire will be known by your name. Take this chain of many forms as well.
1.1.17: One who lights the Nachiketa fire three times, joined with the three, and does the three kinds of work, crosses birth and death. Knowing the bright one born of Brahman, worthy of praise, and seeing him, one reaches lasting peace.
1.1.18: One who knows these three and, knowing them, builds the Nachiketa fire, throws off the ropes of death ahead of time and, beyond sorrow, is glad in heaven.
1.1.19: This is your fire that leads to heaven, Nachiketa, which you chose with your second wish. People will call this fire by your name. Now, Nachiketa, choose your third wish.
1.1.20: When a person dies, there is this doubt. Some say, "He is." Others say, "He is not." I want to know this, taught by you. Of my wishes, this is the third.
1.1.21: Even the gods doubted this long ago. It is not easy to understand; it is a fine point. Choose another wish, Nachiketa. Do not hold me to this one. Let it go.
1.1.22: Even the gods doubted it, and you, Death, say it is not easy to understand. Another teacher like you cannot be found, and no other wish is equal to this one.
1.1.23: Choose sons and grandsons who will live a hundred years. Choose cattle, elephants, gold and horses. Choose wide lands, and live yourself for as many autumns as you like.
1.1.24: If you can think of a wish equal to this, choose it: wealth, and a long life with it. Be great on the wide earth, Nachiketa. I will make you enjoy every desire.
1.1.25: Whatever desires are hard to win in the world of mortals, ask for all of them as you please. Here are lovely women with chariots and music; men cannot win their like. I give them to you; let them serve you. Nachiketa, do not ask about death.
1.1.26: These last until tomorrow, Death, and they wear down the strength of every sense. Even a whole life is short. Keep your horses, and your dancing and singing.
1.1.27: No one is ever satisfied by wealth. Will we lack wealth now that we have seen you? We will live as long as you rule. The wish I choose is that one only.
1.1.28: Once he has come near those who do not age or die, what mortal down here, ageing and knowing it, who has weighed up beauty and pleasure and delight, would enjoy a very long life?
1.1.29: Tell us, Death, the thing people doubt, what happens in the great passing on. This wish goes into what is hidden. Nachiketa chooses no other.
1.2.1: The good is one thing, and the pleasant is another. Both take hold of a person, toward different ends. It goes well for the one who takes the good. The one who chooses the pleasant misses the goal.
1.2.2: The good and the pleasant both come to a person. The steady one looks at both and tells them apart. The steady one chooses the good over the pleasant. The dull one chooses the pleasant, for getting and keeping.
1.2.3: You, Nachiketa, have looked hard at pleasures that are dear and look dear, and let them go. You did not take this chain of wealth in which so many people sink.
1.2.4: These two are far apart and lead different ways: ignorance, and what is known as knowledge. I see Nachiketa wants knowledge. All those pleasures did not pull you away.
1.2.5: Living inside ignorance, sure they are wise and learned, fools go round and round, like the blind led by the blind.
1.2.6: The passing on does not show itself to a careless child, dazed by wealth. "This world is all there is; there is no other," he thinks, and he falls into my hands again and again.
1.2.7: Many never even hear of it. Many who hear of it do not understand. Wonderful is the one who can teach it, and skilled the one who receives it. Wonderful is the one who knows it, taught by the skilled.
1.2.8: Taught by someone who has not understood, it cannot be known well, however much it is thought about. Unless another who knows teaches it, there is no way in, for it is finer than the finest and beyond argument.
1.2.9: This understanding is not reached by argument, dear one. Taught by another, it is easy to know. You have it, and you hold firm to truth. May we find more questioners like you, Nachiketa.
1.2.10: I know that treasure does not last, and the lasting cannot be reached by things that pass. Still, I built the Nachiketa fire with passing things, and so I gained what lasts.
1.2.11: You saw the fulfilment of desire, the ground of the world, the endless reward of rites, the far shore of fearlessness, great and wide praise, and a firm place to stand. Wise Nachiketa, you were steady and let them all go.
1.2.12: The wise one, by turning the mind toward the Self, knows that God who is hard to see, who has entered what is hidden, who sits in the cave and lives in the depths, the first one. Knowing him, he leaves joy and grief behind.
1.2.13: A mortal who hears this and takes it in, who separates the fine Self from the body and reaches it, is glad, for he has found what is worth gladness. I think the door stands open for Nachiketa.
1.2.14: Tell me what you see that is apart from right and wrong, apart from what is done and not done, apart from what has been and what will be.
1.2.15: The word all the Vedas point to, which every discipline speaks of, for which people live as students under a teacher: I will tell you that word in brief. It is Om.
1.2.16: This syllable is Brahman. This syllable is the highest. One who knows this syllable has whatever they wish for.
1.2.17: This is the best support. This is the highest support. One who knows this support is honoured in the world of Brahman.
1.2.18: The knowing Self is not born and does not die. It did not come from anything, and nothing came from it. Unborn, lasting, always, first, it is not killed when the body is killed.
1.2.19: If the killer thinks he kills, and the killed thinks he is killed, neither of them understands. This does not kill, and it is not killed.
1.2.20: Finer than the fine, greater than the great, the Self sits in the heart of every creature. One who is free of wanting sees its greatness, through the clearness of the senses and mind, and is free of grief.
1.2.21: Sitting still, it travels far. Lying down, it goes everywhere. Who but me can know that God, glad and not glad?
1.2.22: Bodiless among bodies, steady among things that shift, great and present everywhere: knowing the Self this way, the wise one does not grieve.
1.2.23: This Self is not reached by teaching, nor by cleverness, nor by much hearing. It is reached by the one who chooses it. To that one the Self shows its own nature.
1.2.24: One who has not turned away from wrong conduct, who is not calm, not collected, whose mind is not at rest, cannot reach it by knowing.
1.2.25: For whom the priest and the warrior are both food, and death is the sauce poured over it: who can know where he is?
1.3.1: Two drink the fruit of what was done well in the world, both entered into the cave, the highest place. The knowers of Brahman call them shade and light, and so do those who keep the five fires and those who build the Nachiketa fire three times.
1.3.2: May we master the Nachiketa fire, the bridge for those who offer, and the highest Brahman that does not decay, the fearless far shore for those who want to cross.
1.3.3: Know the Self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot. Know the intellect as the driver, and the mind as the reins.
1.3.4: The senses, they say, are the horses, and the things of the senses are the roads they run on. The Self joined to body, senses and mind is the one who experiences, the wise say.
1.3.5: When a person has no understanding and his mind is never held, his senses run out of control, like a driver's unbroken horses.
1.3.6: When a person has understanding and his mind is always held, his senses stay in control, like a driver's good horses.
1.3.7: One who has no understanding, who is careless and never clean within, does not reach that place, and comes back into the round of births.
1.3.8: One who has understanding, who is careful and always clean within, reaches that place from which he is not born again.
1.3.9: One whose driver is understanding, and who holds the reins of the mind, reaches the end of the road, the highest place of Vishnu.
1.3.10: Beyond the senses are their objects. Beyond the objects is the mind. Beyond the mind is the intellect. Beyond the intellect is the great self.
1.3.11: Beyond the great is the unmanifest. Beyond the unmanifest is the Person. Beyond the Person there is nothing. That is the end. That is the highest goal.
1.3.12: This Self is hidden in every being and does not shine out. Those who see finely see it, with a sharp and subtle intellect.
1.3.13: The wise one should draw speech into the mind, the mind into the knowing self, the knowing self into the great self, and the great self into the Self at peace.
1.3.14: Arise. Awake. Go to the great teachers and learn. The wise say the path is as sharp as a razor's edge, hard to cross and hard to walk.
1.3.15: Without sound, touch, form or decay, without taste or smell, always, without beginning or end, beyond the great, unmoving: knowing That, one is freed from the mouth of death.
1.3.16: The wise one who hears and tells this first story of Nachiketa, as Death told it, is honoured in the world of Brahman.
1.3.17: One who, made clean, recites this highest secret in a gathering of Brahmins, or at the rite for the dead, gains what is endless. He gains what is endless.
2.1.1: The Self-born cut the openings of the senses facing outward, so a person looks out and not within. A wise one, wanting the deathless, turned his eyes inward and saw the Self.
2.1.2: Children run after outward pleasures and walk into the wide net of death. The wise, knowing what is deathless and sure, do not look for the lasting among the things here that pass.
2.1.3: That by which one knows form, taste, smell, sound, touch and the pleasures of love: what is left here that it does not know? This is That.
2.1.4: That by which one sees both dream and waking: knowing it as the great Self present everywhere, the wise one does not grieve.
2.1.5: One who knows this Self that tastes the honey of life, the living one close at hand, lord of what was and what will be, shrinks from nothing after that. This is That.
2.1.6: The one who was born first, from discipline, born before the waters, who entered the cave and stays there among the elements, and is seen there: This is That.
2.1.7: Aditi, who rises as life itself, made of the gods, who entered the cave and stays there, born together with the elements: This is That.
2.1.8: Agni, who knows all that is born, hidden in the two fire sticks like a child well guarded by mothers, praised every day by people who are awake and make offerings: This is That.
2.1.9: That from which the sun rises and into which it sets, in which all the gods are fixed, beyond which no one passes: This is That.
2.1.10: What is here is there, and what is there is here. One who sees difference here goes from death to death.
2.1.11: This is to be reached by the mind alone: there is no difference here at all. One who sees difference here goes from death to death.
2.1.12: The Person the size of a thumb stands in the middle of the body, lord of what was and what will be. One who knows him shrinks from nothing after that. This is That.
2.1.13: The Person the size of a thumb is like a flame without smoke, lord of what was and what will be. He is here today, and he will be here tomorrow. This is That.
2.1.14: As rain that falls on high ground runs off down the hills, one who sees things as separate runs after them.
2.1.15: As clear water poured into clear water becomes just that, so does the Self of the sage who knows, Gautama.
2.2.1: The city of the unborn one, whose knowing is never bent, has eleven gates. One who attends to him grieves no more, and, set free, is free. This is That.
2.2.2: He is the sun moving in the bright sky, the wind in the middle air, the fire on the altar, the guest in the house. He is in people, in the gods, in what is right, in the sky. He is born in water, born of earth, born in the rite, born on the mountains. He is the true, the vast.
2.2.3: He leads the out-breath upward and pushes the in-breath down. All the gods serve the small one who sits in the middle.
2.2.4: When this one who lives in the body slips away and is freed from the body, what is left here? This is That.
2.2.5: No mortal lives by the out-breath or by the in-breath. People live by something else, on which these two rest.
2.2.6: Now I will tell you about this hidden Brahman that has always been, and what becomes of the self after death, Gautama.
2.2.7: Some go into a womb to take a body. Others go into things that do not move, each according to what they have done and what they have learned.
2.2.8: The one who stays awake in those who sleep, shaping one desire after another: that is the bright, that is Brahman, that is called the deathless. All worlds rest in it, and no one passes beyond it. This is That.
2.2.9: As the one fire, entering the world, takes the shape of whatever it burns, so the one Self inside all beings takes the shape of each, and is also outside them.
2.2.10: As the one air, entering the world, takes the shape of whatever it fills, so the one Self inside all beings takes the shape of each, and is also outside them.
2.2.11: As the sun, the eye of the whole world, is not touched by the faults of the eyes or of what they see, so the one Self inside all beings is not touched by the world's pain, for it stands outside it.
2.2.12: The one ruler, the Self inside all beings, who makes one form into many: the wise who see him in themselves have lasting happiness. Others do not.
2.2.13: The lasting among things that pass, the awareness in all who are aware, the one who answers the wishes of many: the wise who see him in themselves have lasting peace. Others do not.
2.2.14: "This is That," the wise know, the highest happiness, which cannot be put into words. How shall I know it? Does it shine on its own, or by another light?
2.2.15: The sun does not shine there, nor the moon and stars, nor these flashes of lightning, still less this fire. Everything shines after him as he shines. By his light all of this shines.
2.3.1: This is the old fig tree with its roots above and its branches below. That is the bright, that is Brahman, that is called the deathless. All worlds rest in it, and no one passes beyond it. This is That.
2.3.2: Whatever there is, the whole world, came out of life and moves within it. It is a great fear, like a raised thunderbolt. Those who know it become deathless.
2.3.3: From fear of him the fire burns. From fear the sun gives heat. From fear Indra and the wind, and Death as the fifth, run their course.
2.3.4: If a person comes to know it here, before the body falls away, he is free. If not, he takes a body again in the made worlds.
2.3.5: As in a mirror, so it is seen in oneself. As in a dream, so in the world of the ancestors. As in water, so in the world of the gandharvas. As light and shade, so in the world of Brahman.
2.3.6: Knowing that the senses are separate, and that their rising and setting belongs to them alone, the wise one does not grieve.
2.3.7: Higher than the senses is the mind. Higher than the mind is the clear intellect. Above the intellect is the great self, and higher than the great is the unmanifest.
2.3.8: Higher than the unmanifest is the Person, present everywhere and without any marks. Knowing him, a creature is set free and reaches the deathless.
2.3.9: His form is not something the eye can stand before. No one sees him with the eye. He is grasped by the heart, by insight, by the mind. Those who know this become deathless.
2.3.10: When the five senses of knowing rest together with the mind, and the intellect does not stir, that, they say, is the highest state.
2.3.11: This steady holding of the senses is what they call yoga. Then a person becomes watchful, for yoga comes and it goes.
2.3.12: It cannot be reached by speech, or by the mind, or by the eye. How can it be known except by one who says, "It is"?
2.3.13: It is first to be grasped as "It is," and then in its true nature, of the two. Once grasped as "It is," its true nature becomes clear.
2.3.14: When every desire lodged in the heart lets go, the mortal becomes deathless and reaches Brahman here.
2.3.15: When every knot of the heart is cut here, the mortal becomes deathless. This is all the teaching there is.
2.3.16: The heart has a hundred and one channels. One of them goes up through the crown of the head. Going up by it, one reaches the deathless. The others lead out in all directions.
2.3.17: The Person the size of a thumb, the Self within, always sits in the heart of people. Draw him out from your own body with patience, as a stalk is drawn from a reed. Know him as the bright, the deathless. Know him as the bright, the deathless.
2.3.18: So Nachiketa, having received this knowledge from Death, and the whole practice of yoga, reached Brahman, free of stain and free of death. So will anyone else who knows the inner Self this way.
